column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 40: “Be in this world as though you were a stranger”

column2: From Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ took hold of my shoulder and said:

“Be in this world as though you were a stranger, or a traveller passing through.” And Ibn ʿUmar used to say: When evening comes, do not wait for the morning; and when morning comes, do not wait for the evening. Take from your health for your sickness, and from your life for your death. Al-Bukhārī reported it.
Al-Bukhārī recorded this hadith from ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Ṭufāwī told us, al-Aʿmash told us, Mujāhid told me, from Ibn ʿUmar,
and he mentioned it. More than one of the hadith masters have criticised the words “Mujāhid told us”, saying that they are not established. They faulted Ibn al-Madīnī for them and said:

Al-Aʿmash did not hear this hadith from Mujāhid; he heard it only from Layth ibn Abī Sulaym, from him. Al-ʿUqaylī and others mentioned that. Al-Tirmidhī recorded it from the hadith of Layth, from Mujāhid,
adding in it: “and count yourself among the people of the graves”; and he added to Ibn ʿUmar's words: For you do not know, ʿAbdullāh, what your name will be tomorrow.
Ibn Mājah recorded it without mentioning Ibn ʿUmar's saying.

Imam Aḥmad and al-Nasāʾī recorded, from the hadith of al-Awzāʿī, from ʿAbdah ibn Abī Lubābah, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: The Prophet ﷺ took hold of part of my body and said: “Worship Allah as though you see Him, and be in this world as though you were a stranger or a traveller passing through.”
ʿAbdah ibn Abī Lubābah lived in the time of Ibn ʿUmar, and there is disagreement over whether he heard from him.

This hadith is a foundation for shortness of hope in this world. The believer should not take this world as a homeland and dwelling and settle down in it at ease; rather, he should be in it as though he were on the point of a journey, making ready his provisions for departure.

The counsels of the prophets and their followers agree on this. The Exalted says, telling of the believer of Pharaoh's family that he said: “My people, this worldly life is only a passing enjoyment, and the Hereafter is the abode of permanence” [Ghāfir 40:39].
The Prophet ﷺ used to say: “What have I to do with this world? My likeness and the likeness of this world is that of a rider who rested at midday in the shade of a tree, then went on and left it.”

Among the counsels of the Messiah (peace be upon him) to his companions was his saying to them: Pass through it, and do not build it up. It is also narrated that he said: Who would build a house on the waves of the sea? Such is this world, so do not take it as a place to settle.
A man came in to see Abū Dharr and began looking around his house. He said: Abū Dharr, where are your belongings?
He said: We have a house to which we are heading. The man said: But you must have belongings so long as you are here. He said: The owner of the dwelling will not leave us in it.
Some people came in to see one of the righteous and looked around his house. They said to him: We see that your house is the house of a man about to depart. He said: About to depart?
No — I am being driven out.
ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him) used to say: This world has set off and is going away, and the Hereafter has set off and is coming near,
and each of them has its children. So be children of the Hereafter, and do not be children of this world; for today there is action and no reckoning, and tomorrow there is reckoning and no action.

One of the sages said: I marvel at one from whom this world is turning away, and towards whom the Hereafter is coming, yet who busies himself with what is departing and turns away from what is approaching.

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said in his sermon: This world is not your abode of permanence. Allah has decreed passing away for it, and has decreed for its people that they depart from it. How many a thriving, well-secured place will soon fall to ruin,

and how many a contented resident will soon depart! So, may Allah have mercy on you, make your departure from it a good one, with the best of the means of moving on that you have at hand, and “take provision, for the best provision is taqwā” [al-Baqarah 2:197].

Since this world is neither an abode of residence nor a homeland for the believer, his state in it ought to be one of two. Either he is like a stranger residing in a foreign land, whose concern is to gather provision for his return to his homeland,

or he is like a traveller who does not reside anywhere at all, but is journeying night and day towards the land of residence. That is why the Prophet ﷺ counselled Ibn ʿUmar to be in this world in one of these two states.

The first is that the believer regards himself as a stranger in this world: he pictures himself as residing, but in a foreign land. His heart is not attached to the land where he is a stranger; rather, it is attached to his homeland, to which he will return,

and he stays in this world only to finish mending his gear for the return to his homeland. Al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ said: The believer in this world is anxious and sorrowful; his concern is mending his gear.

Whoever is like that in this world has no concern except to gather the provision that will benefit him when he returns to his homeland. He does not compete with the people of the land where he is a stranger for their honour,

nor is he troubled by being humbled among them. Al-Ḥasan said: The believer in this world is like a stranger: he is not troubled by its humiliation and does not compete for its honour. He has his concern, and people have theirs.

When Ādam was created, he and his wife were made to dwell in Paradise; then they were sent down from it, and were promised a return to it, together with the righteous of their offspring. So the believer always yearns for his first homeland, as it has been said:
How many a dwelling a young man grows fond of, / yet his yearning is always for the first dwelling.
One of our shaykhs said:
Come, then, to the Gardens of Eden, for they / are your first dwellings, and there is the encampment;
but we are captives of the enemy — do you think / we shall return to our homelands and be safe?
They have claimed that when a stranger is far away / and his homelands are distant, he is sick with longing;
and what estrangement is greater than ours, / in which the enemies now rule over us?
ʿAṭāʾ al-Salīmī used to say in his supplication: O Allah, have mercy on my estrangement in this world, have mercy on my loneliness in the grave, and have mercy on my standing before You tomorrow.

Al-Ḥasan said: It has reached me that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to his Companions: “My likeness, your likeness and the likeness of this world are those of a people who travelled through a dusty desert until, when they no longer knew whether more of it lay behind them or ahead, they had used up their provisions and worn out their mounts,

and were left in the middle of the desert with no provisions and no beasts of burden, certain that they would perish. While they were in that state, a man came out to them in a fine robe, his head dripping with water.
They said: This man has only recently left fertile land; he has come to you from somewhere close by. When he reached them, he said: What state are you in?
They said: As you see. He said: Tell me, if I guide you to plentiful water and green meadows, what will you do?

They said: We will not disobey you in anything. He said: [Give me] your covenants and pledges by Allah. So they gave him their covenants and pledges by Allah that they would not disobey him in anything. He brought them to water and green meadows and stayed among them as long as Allah willed. Then he said: Come, you people, it is time to move on. They said: To where?

He said: To water unlike your water and to meadows unlike your meadows. The bulk of the people — and they were the majority — said: By Allah, we did not find this until we thought we never would; what would we do with a life better than this?

But a group — and they were the fewest — said: Did you not give this man your covenants and pledges by Allah that you would not disobey him in anything? He told you the truth at the beginning of what he said,

and by Allah he will tell you the truth at the end of it. So he set off with those who followed him, and the rest stayed behind. An enemy got wind of them, and by morning they were either captives or slain.” Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded it.
Imam Aḥmad recorded it from the hadith of ʿAlī ibn Zayd ibn Judʿān, from Yūsuf ibn Mihrān, from Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet ﷺ, with the same meaning in abridged form.

This parable matches perfectly the state of the Prophet ﷺ with his nation. He came to them when the Arabs were the most abased of people, the fewest in number and the worst off, both in their life in this world and in their state in the Hereafter. He called them to take the path of salvation, and the proofs of his truthfulness appeared to them,

just as the truthfulness of the man who came to the people in the desert, whose water had run out and whose mounts had perished, appeared when they saw him in a fine robe, his hair combed and his head dripping with water; and he guided them to water and grassy meadows. They took his appearance and state as evidence of the truth of his words, and followed him.

He promised those who followed him the conquest of the lands of Persia and Rome and the taking of their treasures. He warned them against being deluded by that and halting at it, and commanded them to make do with what suffices them from this world and to strive hard in seeking the Hereafter and preparing for it. They found all he had promised them to be true.
When this world was opened up to them, as he had promised, most people became occupied with amassing it, hoarding it and competing for it; they were content to settle in it and enjoy its appetites,

and abandoned preparing for the Hereafter, which he had commanded them to seek with earnest striving. Only a few people accepted his counsel to strive earnestly in seeking the Hereafter and preparing for it.
This small group was saved and joined their Prophet in the Hereafter, since they followed his path in this world, accepted his counsel and carried out what he commanded.

As for most people, they remained in the intoxication of this world and of vying for more of it, and that distracted them from the Hereafter until death took them by surprise in this heedless state. So they perished, and became either slain or captives.

How excellent is the saying of Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh al-Rāzī: This world is Satan's wine; whoever becomes drunk on it will not come to his senses except in the camp of the dead, full of regret among the losers.

The second state is that the believer regards himself in this world as a traveller who does not reside anywhere at all, but journeys on, crossing the stages of the journey until it brings him to its end, which is death.

Whoever is in this state in this world has as his concern only gathering provision for the journey, and has no interest in amassing the goods of this world. That is why the Prophet ﷺ counselled a number of his Companions that what they took from this world should be like a rider's provisions.
Muḥammad ibn Wāsiʿ was asked: How are you this morning?
He said: What do you think of a man who travels one stage closer to the Hereafter every day?
Al-Ḥasan said: You are nothing but a collection of days; whenever a day passes, part of you passes.

He also said: Son of Ādam, you are between two mounts that hurry you along: the day hurries you to the night, and the night to the day, until they deliver you to the Hereafter. Who, then, son of Ādam, is in greater danger than you? And he said: Death is tied to your forelocks, and this world is being rolled up behind you.

Dāwūd al-Ṭāʾī said: Night and day are stages at which people halt, stage after stage, until they bring them to the end of their journey. If you can send ahead provision at every stage for what lies beyond it,

do so; for the journey will soon be cut short, and the matter is swifter than that. So take provision for your journey and settle whatever affairs you have to settle; it is as if the matter had already taken you by surprise.
One of the Salaf wrote to a brother of his: My brother, you imagine that you are staying put, but in fact you are travelling without pause, and are being driven on at a rapid pace.
Death is coming towards you, and this world is being rolled up behind you. What has passed of your life will not come back to you until it returns to confront you on the Day of Mutual Loss and Gain.
Your way in this world is a traveller's way, / and every traveller must have provision;
a man must carry arms with him, / above all if he fears the assault of a conqueror.

One of the sages said: How can someone rejoice in this world when his day tears down his month, his month tears down his year, and his year tears down his life? How can someone rejoice when his life is leading him to his appointed term and his living is leading him to his death?
Al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ said to a man: How many years have passed over you?

He said: Sixty years. He said: So for sixty years you have been travelling towards your Lord, and you are about to arrive. The man said: To Allah we belong, and to Him we return. Al-Fuḍayl said: Do you know what that means? You are saying: I am Allah's servant, and I am returning to Him.

Whoever knows that he is Allah's servant and that he is returning to Him, let him know that he will be made to stand before Him; whoever knows that he will be made to stand, let him know that he will be questioned; and whoever knows that he will be questioned, let him prepare an answer for the questioning. The man said: Then what is the way out?
He said: It is easy. He said: What is it?

He said: Do well in what remains, and you will be forgiven what has passed; for if you do ill in what remains, you will be taken to task both for what has passed and for what remains. On this someone said:
A man who has travelled for sixty years / towards a watering place is near to reaching it.
One of the sages said: Whoever has the nights and days for his mounts is carried along by them even if he does not travel. On this someone said:
These days are nothing but stages / through which death's herald drives us on towards his goal;
and the strangest thing, if you reflect, is that they / are stages being folded up while the traveller sits still.
Another poet said:
Alas for my soul, from a day that leads it / to the camp of the dead, and a night that drives it on!

Al-Ḥasan said: Night and day have never ceased to be swift in diminishing lives and bringing appointed terms near. How far they are from lasting! They kept company with Nūḥ, ʿĀd, Thamūd and many generations in between,

and these have come before their Lord and arrived at their deeds, while night and day remain fresh and new, unworn by all they have passed through, ready to do to those who remain what they did to those who have gone.

Al-Awzāʿī wrote to a brother of his: To proceed. You are surrounded on every side; and know that you are being carried along every day and night. So be wary of Allah and of standing before Him, and of that being your final meeting with Him. Peace.
We travel towards our appointed terms at every moment; / our days are being rolled up, and they are stages.
I have seen nothing so true as death, yet it seems, / when hopes step over it, a falsehood.
How ugly is negligence in the time of youth — / how much more so when grey hair covers the head!
Depart from this world with a provision of taqwā; / your life is but days, and they are few.

As for Ibn ʿUmar's counsel (may Allah be pleased with them both), it is taken from this hadith that he narrated, and it contains the utmost shortness of hope: when a person reaches the evening he does not wait for the morning, and when he reaches the morning he does not wait for the evening,

but thinks that his appointed term will overtake him before then. More than one of the scholars have explained zuhd in this world in this way. Al-Marrūdhī said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh — meaning Aḥmad: What is zuhd in this world?
He said: Shortness of hope: one who, when he wakes in the morning, says, I will not live to the evening. He said: Sufyān said the same.
Abū ʿAbdillāh was asked: What can we seek help from in shortening our hope?
He said: We do not know; it comes only by Allah's granting of success (tawfīq).
Al-Ḥasan said: Three scholars met, and they said to one of them: What is your hope?
He said: No month has come upon me but I thought I would die in it. His two companions said: That is still hope. They said to another of them: What is your hope?
He said: No week has come upon me but I thought I would die in it. His two companions said: That is still hope. They said to the third: What is your hope?
He said: What hope has one whose soul is in another's hand?
Dāwūd al-Ṭāʾī said: I asked ʿAṭwān ibn ʿAmr al-Tamīmī: What is shortness of hope?

He said: The space between one breath and the next. This was told to al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ, and he wept and said: He means that he breathes and fears he will die before his breath is finished. ʿAṭwān was truly on his guard against death.
One of the Salaf said: I have never once gone to sleep and told myself that I would wake from it.
Ḥabīb Abū Muḥammad used to give, every day, the instructions a dying man gives at his death, about the washing of his body and the like, and he would weep every morning and every evening.
His wife was asked about his weeping, and she said: By Allah, he fears when evening comes that he will not see the morning, and when morning comes that he will not see the evening.

Whenever Muḥammad ibn Wāsiʿ wanted to sleep, he would say to his family: I entrust you to Allah; perhaps this will be my death, from which I will not rise. This was his habit whenever he wanted to sleep.

Bakr al-Muzanī said: If any of you can manage never to spend the night without his will written by his head, let him do so; for he does not know — perhaps he will spend the night among the people of this world and wake among the people of the Hereafter.
When Uways was asked, “How is time treating you?”,

he would say: How is time treating a man who, when evening comes, thinks he will not see the morning, and when morning comes, thinks he will not see the evening — and is then given the tidings of Paradise or the Fire?
ʿAwn ibn ʿAbdullāh said: Whoever counts tomorrow as part of his lifespan has not given death its true place.

How many a person greets a day he will not complete, and how many a person hopes for a tomorrow he will not reach! If you could see the appointed term and its course, you would detest hope and its delusion. He used to say: Among the most beneficial of the believer's days for him in this world is the day he thought he would not live to the end of.

There was a devout woman in Makkah who, when evening came, would say: My soul, tonight is your night; you have no other night but this — and she would strive. When morning came she would say: My soul, today is your day; you have no other day but this — and she would strive.

Bakr al-Muzanī said: If you want your prayer to benefit you, say: Perhaps I will never pray another. This is taken from what is narrated of the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: “Pray the prayer of one bidding farewell.”

Maʿrūf al-Karkhī had the call to begin the prayer given, then said to a man: Go forward and lead us in prayer. The man said: If I lead you in this prayer, I will not lead you in any other. Maʿrūf said: And you are telling yourself that you will pray another prayer?
We seek refuge with Allah from long hope, for it keeps one from the best of deeds.
One of them knocked at the door of a brother of his and asked for him. He was told: He is not at home. He said: When will he be back?
A slave girl of the household said to him: When a man's soul is in another's hand, who can know when he will be back? Among some verses of Abū al-ʿAtāhiyah:
I do not know, though I hope for a long life, / whether, when morning comes, I shall live till evening.
Do you not see that with every day's morning / your life is shorter than it was the day before?

He took this second verse from what is narrated of Abū al-Dardāʾ and al-Ḥasan, that they said: Son of Ādam, you have never ceased tearing down your life since you dropped from your mother's womb. Among what one of the Salaf recited:
We rejoice in the days we pass through, / yet every day gone by brings the appointed term nearer.
So work for yourself, striving, before death comes; / profit and loss lie only in deeds.
His words, “Take from your health for your sickness, and from your life for your death,” mean: make the most of righteous deeds in health before sickness comes between you and them,

and in life before death comes between you and them. In one narration: “For you do not know, ʿAbdullāh, what your name will be tomorrow,” meaning: perhaps tomorrow you will be among the dead and not among the living.

The meaning of this counsel has been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ by several routes. In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, the Prophet ﷺ said: “There are two blessings in which many people are cheated: health and free time.”

In al-Ḥākim's Ṣaḥīḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to a man while admonishing him: “Make the most of five things before five others: your youth before your old age, your health before your sickness, your wealth before your poverty, your free time before your busyness, and your life before your death.”

Ghunaym ibn Qays said: In the early days of Islam we used to admonish one another: Son of Ādam, work in your free time before your busyness, in your youth for your old age, in your health for your sickness, in your worldly life for your Hereafter,
and in your life for your death.
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ:
“Hasten to do deeds before six things: the rising of the sun from where it sets, the smoke, the Dajjāl, the Beast, what befalls one of you in particular, or what befalls people in general.”
In al-Tirmidhī, from him, from the Prophet ﷺ: “Hasten to do deeds before seven things. Are you waiting for anything but poverty that makes you forget,

wealth that makes you transgress, illness that ruins, old age that makes you senile, death that comes swiftly, the Dajjāl — the worst absent thing that is awaited — or the Hour? And the Hour is more grievous and more bitter.”

What is meant by this is that all these things hinder one from deeds. Some of them distract one from them and concern the individual in particular, such as his poverty, his wealth, his illness, his old age and his death; and some are general, such as the coming of the Hour and the emergence of the Dajjāl; and likewise unsettling trials, as has come in another hadith:
“Hasten to do deeds before trials like portions of the dark night.”

After some of these general events no deed is of any benefit, as the Exalted says: “On the day some of your Lord's signs come, no soul will benefit from its faith if it did not believe before or earn some good through its faith” [al-Anʿām 6:158].
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “The Hour will not come until the sun rises from where it sets.
When it rises and the people see it, they will all believe; and that is when no soul will benefit from its faith if it did not believe before or earn some good through its faith.”

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from him, the Prophet ﷺ said: “There are three things which, once they have appeared, no soul will benefit from its faith if it did not believe before or earn some good through its faith: the rising of the sun from where it sets, the Dajjāl, and the Beast of the Earth.”
It also has, from him, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever repents before the sun rises from where it sets, Allah will accept his repentance.”

And from Abū Mūsā, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah stretches out His hand by night so that the one who did wrong by day may repent, and stretches out His hand by day so that the one who did wrong by night may repent, until the sun rises from where it sets.”

Imam Aḥmad, al-Nasāʾī, al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah recorded from the hadith of Ṣafwān ibn ʿAssāl that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah has opened a door towards the west, seventy years wide, for repentance; it will not be closed until the sun rises from it.”
In the Musnad, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr and Muʿāwiyah, the Prophet ﷺ
said: “Repentance will continue to be accepted until the sun rises from the west. When it rises, every heart will be sealed with what is in it, and people will be relieved of deeds.”
It is narrated that ʿĀʾishah said: When the first of the signs appears, the pens will be thrown down, the recording angels will be held back, and bodies will bear witness to deeds.
Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī recorded it. Kathīr ibn Murrah, Yazīd ibn Shurayḥ and others of the Salaf said likewise: When the sun rises from where it sets, hearts will be sealed with what is in them,

the recording angels and deeds will be taken up, and the angels will be commanded not to write any deed. Sufyān al-Thawrī said: When the sun rises from where it sets, the angels will fold up their scrolls and lay down their pens.

The believer must therefore hasten to do righteous deeds before he becomes unable to do them and is prevented from them, whether by illness or death, or by being overtaken by one of these signs with which no deed is accepted.
Abū Ḥāzim said: The merchandise of the Hereafter is unsold now, but soon it will be in demand, and then neither little nor much of it will be obtainable.
Once a person is prevented from deeds, nothing remains to him but remorse and regret over them. He wishes he could return to a state in which he could do them, but the wish does not benefit him.

The Exalted says: “Turn to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes upon you, after which you will not be helped. And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you are unaware. [Do so] lest a soul should say: Alas for me, for what I neglected in regard to Allah! I was among the mockers. Or lest it say: If only Allah had guided me, I would have been among the God-fearing. Or lest it say, when it sees the punishment: If only I had another chance, so that I might be among those who do good!” [al-Zumar 39:54–58].

And the Exalted says: “Until, when death comes to one of them, he says: My Lord, send me back, that I may do right in what I left behind. No! It is only a word he speaks; and behind them is a barrier until the day they are raised” [al-Muʾminūn 23:99–100].

And He, the Mighty and Majestic, says: “Spend from what We have provided for you before death comes to one of you and he says: My Lord, if only You would delay me for a short while, so that I might give charity and be among the righteous. But Allah will never delay a soul when its appointed term has come, and Allah is Aware of what you do” [al-Munāfiqūn 63:10–11].
In al-Tirmidhī, from Abū Hurayrah as marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ): “No one dies but he regrets.” They said: What is his regret?
He said: “If he did well, he regrets that he did not do more; and if he did ill, he regrets that he did not seek to make amends.”
Since this is how matters stand, the believer must make the most of what remains of his life. That is why it has been said: What remains of the believer's life is beyond price.
Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: Every day the believer lives is a gain. Bakr al-Muzanī said: There is no day that Allah brings out into the world but it says:

Son of Ādam, make the most of me, for perhaps you will have no day after me; and no night but it calls out: Son of Ādam, make the most of me, for perhaps you will have no night after me. One of them said:
In your free time, seize the merit of bowing in prayer, / for perhaps your death will come suddenly.
How many a healthy man have you seen, free of illness, / whose healthy soul departed all at once!
Maḥmūd al-Warrāq said:
Your yesterday has passed, a witness of upright standing, / and a new day has followed it for you.
If yesterday you committed some wrong, / follow it with good, and you will be praised.
If you make amends today, its benefit will return / to you; but yesterday, once past, will not return.
Do not put off doing good from one day to the next; / perhaps tomorrow will come and you will be gone.
